sectionTitle: Carbon compounds as fuels and feedstock
topic: Carbon compounds as fuels and feedstock

specStatements.text: Crude oil is a finite resource found in rocks. Crude oil is the remains of an ancient biomass consisting mainly of plankton that was buried in mud.
Crude oil is a mixture of a very large number of compounds. Most of the compounds in crude oil are hydrocarbons, which are molecules made up of hydrogen and carbon atoms only.
Most of the hydrocarbons in crude oil are hydrocarbons called alkanes. The general formula for the homologous series of alkanes is Cₙ H₂ₙ₊₂
The first four members of the alkanes are methane, ethane, propane and butane.
Alkane molecules can be represented in the following forms:
C₂ H₆ or
Students should be able to recognise substances as alkanes given their formulae in these forms.
Students do not need to know the names of specific alkanes other than methane, ethane, propane and butane.
The many hydrocarbons in crude oil may be separated into fractions, each of which contains molecules with a similar number of carbon atoms, by fractional distillation.
The fractions can be processed to produce fuels and feedstock for the petrochemical industry.
Many of the fuels on which we depend for our modern lifestyle, such as petrol, diesel oil, kerosene, heavy fuel oil and liquefied petroleum gases, are produced from crude oil.
Many useful materials on which modern life depends are produced by the petrochemical industry, such as solvents, lubricants, polymers, detergents.
The vast array of natural and synthetic carbon compounds occur due to the ability of carbon atoms to form families of similar compounds.
Students should be able to explain how fractional distillation works in terms of evaporation and condensation.
Knowledge of the names of other specific fractions or fuels is not required.
Some properties of hydrocarbons depend on the size of their molecules, including boiling point, viscosity and flammability. These properties influence how hydrocarbons are used as fuels.
Students should be able to recall how boiling point, viscosity and flammability change with increasing molecular size.
The combustion of hydrocarbon fuels releases energy. During combustion, the carbon and hydrogen in the fuels are oxidised. The complete combustion of a hydrocarbon produces carbon dioxide and water.
Students should be able to write balanced equations for the complete combustion of hydrocarbons with a given formula.
Knowledge of trends in properties of hydrocarbons is limited to:
boiling points
viscosity
flammability.
Hydrocarbons can be broken down (cracked) to produce smaller, more useful molecules.
Cracking can be done by various methods including catalytic cracking and steam cracking.
Students should be able to describe in general terms the conditions used for catalytic cracking and steam cracking.
The products of cracking include alkanes and another type of hydrocarbon called alkenes.
Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes and react with bromine water, which is used as a test for alkenes.
Students should be able to recall the colour change when bromine water reacts with an alkene.
There is a high demand for fuels with small molecules and so some of the products of cracking are useful as fuels.
Alkenes are used to produce polymers and as starting materials for the production of many other chemicals.
Students should be able to balance chemical equations as examples of cracking given the formulae of the reactants and products.
Students should be able to give examples to illustrate the usefulness of cracking. They should also be able to explain how modern life depends on the uses of hydrocarbons.
(For Combined Science: Trilogy and Synergy students do not need to know the formulae or names of individual alkenes.)

scopeNotes.statement: Students do not need to know the names of specific alkanes other than methane, ethane, propane and butane.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only methane, ethane, propane and butane are ever named. Larger alkanes appear only as formulae supplied inside the question itself (C₅H₁₂, C₇H₁₆, C₈H₁₈, C₁₀H₂₂), and no item asks a student to name or recognise a name such as pentane or octane. Where a longer alkane is a distractor it is written as a formula, so knowing or not knowing its name neither helps nor harms.

scopeNotes.statement: Knowledge of the names of other specific fractions or fuels is not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The only fuels named anywhere in this content are the five the specification itself lists: petrol, diesel oil, kerosene, heavy fuel oil and liquefied petroleum gases. Distractors that are not crude oil fuels (bioethanol, charcoal, hydrogen) are named because a student is expected to reject them on origin, not because they are extra fractions to memorise. No item asks for the name of a fraction such as naphtha or bitumen.

scopeNotes.statement: Knowledge of trends in properties of hydrocarbons is limited to:
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every trend item in this content is restricted to the three properties the specification lists immediately below this line – boiling points, viscosity and flammability. No question asks about trends in density, colour, solubility, melting point or conductivity except as distractors that a student rejects precisely because they lie outside the listed three.

scopeNotes.statement: (For Combined Science: Trilogy and Synergy students do not need to know the formulae or names of individual alkenes.)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Alkenes are treated only as a class: 'another type of hydrocarbon called alkenes', more reactive than alkanes, decolourising bromine water, and used to make polymers. Where an alkene formula appears in a cracking equation it is printed in the question stem or in the options, so no student has to recall or generate it. No item requires the name ethene, propene or butene.

concepts.definition: A finite resource found in rocks; the remains of an ancient biomass consisting mainly of plankton that was buried in mud.
A resource that is being used up far faster than it is formed, so the supply will eventually run out.
Material that was once living. The biomass that formed crude oil consisted mainly of plankton.
Two or more substances that are not chemically joined together. Crude oil is a mixture of a very large number of compounds.
A molecule made up of hydrogen and carbon atoms only.
The homologous series that most of the hydrocarbons in crude oil belong to, with the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
A family of similar compounds that share a general formula, such as the alkanes.
A formula that gives the number of each kind of atom in terms of n. For alkanes it is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
A formula such as C₂H₆ that gives the number of atoms of each element in one molecule.
A drawing that shows every atom in a molecule and the covalent bonds between them.
The first alkane, CH₄; one carbon atom joined to four hydrogen atoms.
The second alkane, C₂H₆; two carbon atoms joined to each other and to six hydrogen atoms.
The third alkane, C₃H₈.
The fourth alkane, C₄H₁₀.
A part of crude oil separated by fractional distillation, containing molecules with a similar number of carbon atoms.
Separating the hydrocarbons in crude oil into fractions by evaporating the oil and condensing each fraction at a different temperature.
Turning a liquid into a vapour. The heated crude oil evaporates before it enters the fractionating column.
Turning a vapour back into a liquid. Each fraction condenses where the column has cooled to its boiling point.
A raw material fed into a chemical process. Crude oil fractions are used as feedstock for the petrochemical industry.
The industry that turns crude oil fractions into useful materials such as solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents.
The temperature at which a liquid boils. For hydrocarbons it increases as the molecules get larger.
How thick a liquid is and how easily it flows. Hydrocarbons become more viscous as the molecules get larger.
How easily a substance catches fire. Hydrocarbons become less flammable as the molecules get larger.
Burning a fuel in oxygen, which releases energy.
Burning a hydrocarbon in plenty of oxygen so that the only products are carbon dioxide and water.
Gain of oxygen. During combustion both the carbon and the hydrogen in the fuel are oxidised.
Breaking down hydrocarbons to produce smaller, more useful molecules.
Cracking in which hydrocarbon vapour is passed over a hot catalyst.
Cracking in which hydrocarbon vapour is mixed with steam and heated to a very high temperature.
A type of hydrocarbon produced by cracking. Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes.
Adding bromine water to a hydrocarbon. An alkene turns the orange bromine water colourless; an alkane does not.
A very long molecule made by joining many small molecules together. Alkenes are used to produce polymers.

misconceptions.question: What was crude oil formed from?
misconceptions.correct: The remains of an ancient biomass consisting mainly of plankton that was buried in mud.
misconceptions.misconception: Crude oil formed from dinosaurs and other large animals that died and rotted underground.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Crude oil is called a fossil fuel, and dinosaurs are the fossils children meet first, so the two ideas become attached to one another.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is precise: the biomass was mainly plankton, tiny marine organisms. Large animals contributed effectively nothing to crude oil.

misconceptions.question: What was crude oil formed from?
misconceptions.correct: An ancient biomass of mainly plankton buried in mud.
misconceptions.misconception: Crude oil formed from ancient forests of land plants that were buried in swamps.
misconceptions.whyItArises: This is a real fossil fuel origin story – it is how coal formed – so students who have learned it apply it to every fossil fuel.
misconceptions.correction: Coal came from land plants; crude oil came from marine plankton buried in mud. The two fuels have different origins and are worth keeping apart.

misconceptions.question: Why is crude oil called a finite resource?
misconceptions.correct: It is being used up far faster than any new crude oil can form.
misconceptions.misconception: Crude oil is renewable, because new oil is forming underground all the time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students hear that oil is still being made and conclude that supply is being topped up at a useful rate.
misconceptions.correction: Formation takes millions of years. Compared with the rate at which we extract it, the rate of formation is effectively zero, so the resource is finite.

misconceptions.question: Why is crude oil called a finite resource?
misconceptions.correct: Supplies will run out because it is used far faster than it forms.
misconceptions.misconception: Finite means that crude oil is only found in a few countries.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Finite' is read as 'limited in where you can get it' rather than 'limited in total amount'.
misconceptions.correction: Finite is about total quantity and rate of replacement, not geography. Even if oil were found everywhere it would still be finite.

misconceptions.question: What is a hydrocarbon?
misconceptions.correct: A molecule made up of hydrogen and carbon atoms only.
misconceptions.misconception: A hydrocarbon is a molecule containing hydrogen, carbon and oxygen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most familiar organic molecules met later – alcohols, sugars, carboxylic acids – do contain oxygen, so oxygen feels like part of the package.
misconceptions.correction: The word 'only' is doing the work. As soon as a third element such as oxygen is present the molecule is not a hydrocarbon.

misconceptions.question: Is every carbon compound a hydrocarbon?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only compounds of hydrogen and carbon alone are hydrocarbons.
misconceptions.misconception: Any compound that contains carbon is a hydrocarbon.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 'carbon' half of the word is noticed and the 'hydro' half is treated as decoration.
misconceptions.correction: Both elements must be present and no others. Carbon dioxide and ethanol contain carbon but are not hydrocarbons.

misconceptions.question: Is crude oil a single compound?
misconceptions.correct: No, it is a mixture of a very large number of compounds.
misconceptions.misconception: Crude oil is one compound with a single fixed formula.
misconceptions.whyItArises: It arrives as one black liquid with one name, and named substances in chemistry usually have one formula.
misconceptions.correction: Crude oil is a mixture: its compounds are not chemically joined, which is exactly why they can be separated by fractional distillation.

misconceptions.question: Is crude oil an element, a compound or a mixture?
misconceptions.correct: A mixture of a very large number of compounds, mostly hydrocarbons.
misconceptions.misconception: Crude oil is a compound made from the elements carbon and hydrogen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know it is 'made of carbon and hydrogen' and jump to compound, because compounds are what elements make.
misconceptions.correction: Each hydrocarbon molecule is a compound, but the oil itself is a mixture of very many different such compounds.

misconceptions.question: What is the general formula of the alkanes?
misconceptions.correct: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
misconceptions.misconception: The general formula of the alkanes is CₙH₂ₙ.
misconceptions.whyItArises: CₙH₂ₙ is the tidier pattern and is the formula of the alkenes, which is met alongside it, so the two get swapped.
misconceptions.correction: Alkanes are saturated and carry two extra hydrogen atoms at the ends of the chain: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. CₙH₂ₙ belongs to the alkenes.

misconceptions.question: What is the general formula of the alkanes?
misconceptions.correct: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
misconceptions.misconception: The general formula is CₙH₂ₙ₊₁, or CₙH₂ₙ₋₂.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The '+2' is remembered as 'a small number added on' without recalling which, so ±1 and −2 look equally reasonable.
misconceptions.correction: Check against a known member: methane has one carbon and four hydrogens, and 2 × 1 + 2 = 4. Only +2 works.

misconceptions.question: What are the first four alkanes?
misconceptions.correct: Methane, ethane, propane and butane.
misconceptions.misconception: The first four alkanes are methane, ethene, propene and butene.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The prefixes are shared between the two families, so only the -ane/-ene ending distinguishes them and it is easily lost.
misconceptions.correction: The ending carries the family: -ane means alkane, -ene means alkene. The first four alkanes all end in -ane.

misconceptions.question: What are the first four alkanes?
misconceptions.correct: Methane, ethane, propane and butane.
misconceptions.misconception: The list runs methane, ethane, propane, pentane – or the order of propane and butane is swapped.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The prefixes meth-, eth-, prop-, but- are not a familiar counting sequence, unlike pent- and hex- which sound like five and six.
misconceptions.correction: The first four are methane (1 C), ethane (2 C), propane (3 C) and butane (4 C), in that order. Pentane would be the fifth.

misconceptions.question: What does a displayed formula show that a molecular formula does not?
misconceptions.correct: It shows the covalent bonds between the atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: A displayed formula just shows how many atoms of each element there are.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both representations show the same atoms, so the atom count is the feature that stands out; the lines are treated as decoration.
misconceptions.correction: The atom count is exactly what the molecular formula already gives. The extra information in a displayed formula is the bonding – which atom is joined to which.

misconceptions.question: What do the lines in a displayed formula represent?
misconceptions.correct: Covalent bonds between pairs of atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: The lines show the charges on the atoms, or their relative masses.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams in ionic bonding carry charges, and students transfer that habit to covalent drawings.
misconceptions.correction: Alkanes are covalent molecules with no charges. Each line is one shared pair of electrons – one covalent bond.

misconceptions.question: How are the atoms bonded in ethane, C₂H₆?
misconceptions.correct: A single carbon–carbon bond and six carbon–hydrogen bonds.
misconceptions.misconception: Ethane contains a carbon–carbon double bond.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two carbon atoms next to each other suggests a double bond, especially once alkenes have been drawn.
misconceptions.correction: Ethane is an alkane and is saturated: every bond is single. C₂H₆ has seven single bonds in total.

misconceptions.question: How many covalent bonds are in a molecule of ethane?
misconceptions.correct: Seven: one C–C bond and six C–H bonds.
misconceptions.misconception: The number of bonds equals the number of atoms in the formula.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Counting atoms is easy and gives a number, so it substitutes for counting the lines in the structure.
misconceptions.correction: Bonds join atoms, so there is no reason for the two counts to match. Draw the molecule and count the lines: ethane has seven.

misconceptions.question: Is C₅H₁₀ an alkane?
misconceptions.correct: No. An alkane with 5 carbons would be C₅H₁₂.
misconceptions.misconception: C₅H₁₀ is an alkane because it is made of carbon and hydrogen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Being a hydrocarbon is confused with being an alkane; the general formula is not applied as a test.
misconceptions.correction: Every hydrocarbon is not an alkane. Test the formula against CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: with n = 5 that requires 12 hydrogens, not 10.

misconceptions.question: What is fractional distillation based on?
misconceptions.correct: Differences in the boiling points of the hydrocarbons.
misconceptions.misconception: The fractions are separated because they react differently in the column.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Anything happening in a large industrial tower is assumed to be a chemical change.
misconceptions.correction: Fractional distillation is a physical separation. Nothing reacts; the hydrocarbons are sorted by the temperature at which they condense.

misconceptions.question: What is fractional distillation based on?
misconceptions.correct: Differences in boiling point between the hydrocarbons.
misconceptions.misconception: The heavier fractions simply sink to the bottom of the column because they are denser.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The heaviest fractions really are collected at the bottom, so density looks like a sufficient explanation.
misconceptions.correction: They are collected low down because they condense first, at the highest temperatures. The material moving through the column is vapour, not settling liquid.

misconceptions.question: What is in one fraction of crude oil?
misconceptions.correct: Molecules with a similar number of carbon atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: Each fraction is a single pure compound.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fractions are given single names like petrol and kerosene, and named substances usually mean one compound.
misconceptions.correction: A fraction is still a mixture. What its molecules share is a similar number of carbon atoms, so they boil over a narrow range.

misconceptions.question: What do molecules in the same fraction share?
misconceptions.correct: A similar number of carbon atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: They all contain exactly the same number of hydrogen atoms.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Similar' is upgraded to 'identical', and hydrogen is chosen because it is the larger number in the formula.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says a similar number of carbon atoms. The count is not identical, and it is carbon that defines the fraction.

misconceptions.question: What two changes of state happen in fractional distillation?
misconceptions.correct: Evaporation of the oil and condensation of each fraction.
misconceptions.misconception: The oil is melted and each fraction then freezes out at a different temperature.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Melting and freezing are the pair of changes students meet first, and any temperature-based separation is mapped onto them.
misconceptions.correction: Crude oil is already a liquid. It is evaporated, and the fractions are recovered by condensing the vapour back to liquid.

misconceptions.question: Where is a fractionating column hottest?
misconceptions.correct: At the bottom, where the hot vapour enters.
misconceptions.misconception: The top of the column is the hottest part, because heat rises.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Heat rises' is a genuine and useful idea about convection, applied here to a column that is deliberately cooled towards the top.
misconceptions.correction: The vapour is fed in hot at the bottom and cools as it rises, so the top is coolest. That gradient is what sorts the fractions.

misconceptions.question: What are the fractions used for?
misconceptions.correct: Fuels, and feedstock for the petrochemical industry.
misconceptions.misconception: Every fraction is burned as a fuel.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fuels are the use of crude oil that students meet at home and in the news, so it eclipses the feedstock role.
misconceptions.correction: Fuels are only half of it. Fractions are also fed into the petrochemical industry to make solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents.

misconceptions.question: What does feedstock mean?
misconceptions.correct: A raw material fed into a chemical process to make other substances.
misconceptions.misconception: Feedstock is another word for fuel.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two words appear in the same sentence of the specification and both describe something being 'fed' into a process.
misconceptions.correction: A fuel is burned for energy; a feedstock is a starting material converted into new products such as polymers and detergents.

misconceptions.question: Which fuels are produced from crude oil?
misconceptions.correct: Petrol, diesel oil, kerosene, heavy fuel oil and liquefied petroleum gases.
misconceptions.misconception: Bioethanol and biodiesel are fractions of crude oil.
misconceptions.whyItArises: They are liquid fuels used in engines, so they are filed alongside petrol and diesel without asking where they come from.
misconceptions.correction: Bio- fuels are made from crops by fermentation or from plant oils. They are not obtained from crude oil at all.

misconceptions.question: What does the petrochemical industry make?
misconceptions.correct: Solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents.
misconceptions.misconception: The petrochemical industry makes the fuels: petrol, diesel oil and kerosene.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Petro-' is read as petrol, so the industry is assumed to be the one that makes it.
misconceptions.correction: The fuels are listed separately in the specification. The petrochemical industry uses fractions as feedstock to make materials, not fuels.

misconceptions.question: Why are there so many carbon compounds?
misconceptions.correct: Carbon atoms can form families of similar compounds.
misconceptions.misconception: Carbon forms many compounds because it has many isotopes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are well known, so isotopes are the first special thing about carbon that comes to mind.
misconceptions.correction: Isotopes differ only in neutrons and behave identically chemically. The variety comes from carbon atoms bonding to each other in families of similar compounds.

misconceptions.question: How do carbon atoms build so many different compounds?
misconceptions.correct: By joining to one another to form families of similar compounds.
misconceptions.misconception: Carbon atoms bond ionically to each other to make long chains.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ionic bonding is the strong bonding students meet first, so it is offered whenever strong bonds are needed.
misconceptions.correction: Carbon atoms share electrons: the bonds in hydrocarbons are covalent. Ionic bonding needs a metal and a non-metal.

misconceptions.question: How does boiling point change as hydrocarbon molecules get larger?
misconceptions.correct: It increases.
misconceptions.misconception: Larger hydrocarbon molecules have lower boiling points.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Petrol, which evaporates readily, is the most familiar fraction, and 'light' fuels are assumed to be the ones that boil at higher temperatures.
misconceptions.correction: Larger molecules attract each other more strongly, so more energy is needed to separate them. Boiling point rises with molecular size.

misconceptions.question: How does flammability change as hydrocarbon molecules get larger?
misconceptions.correct: It decreases.
misconceptions.misconception: Bigger molecules are more flammable because they contain more carbon to burn.
misconceptions.whyItArises: More fuel per molecule sounds like more burning, and energy released is confused with ease of ignition.
misconceptions.correction: Flammability is about how easily the fuel ignites. Large molecules are hard to vaporise, so they are much harder to light.

misconceptions.question: How does viscosity change as hydrocarbon molecules get larger?
misconceptions.correct: It increases, so the liquid flows less easily.
misconceptions.misconception: Larger molecules make the liquid runnier, because heavy things pour faster.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Viscosity is an unfamiliar word and is guessed at from everyday experience of pouring rather than from molecular attraction.
misconceptions.correction: Longer molecules tangle and attract each other more, so thick fractions such as heavy fuel oil pour very slowly.

misconceptions.question: What does viscosity measure?
misconceptions.correct: How easily a liquid flows.
misconceptions.misconception: Viscosity is how easily a liquid catches fire.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Viscosity, volatility and flammability are three long words met together, and they blur into a single vague idea of 'how the fuel behaves'.
misconceptions.correction: Viscosity is about flow alone. A viscous liquid is thick and pours slowly; it says nothing directly about ignition.

misconceptions.question: Which properties of hydrocarbons depend on molecular size?
misconceptions.correct: Boiling point, viscosity and flammability.
misconceptions.misconception: Colour, density and electrical conductivity change with molecular size.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Any list of properties feels equally plausible when the specific three have not been committed to memory.
misconceptions.correction: The specification limits the trends to boiling point, viscosity and flammability. Hydrocarbons do not conduct electricity at all.

misconceptions.question: Why are gases from crude oil used in portable stoves?
misconceptions.correct: They are highly flammable, so they ignite easily.
misconceptions.misconception: A good portable fuel needs a high boiling point so that it does not escape.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Safety is associated with something that will not evaporate, so a high boiling point is assumed to be desirable.
misconceptions.correction: A stove needs a fuel that vaporises and ignites easily. Small molecules with low boiling points are exactly what is wanted.

misconceptions.question: What are the products of complete combustion of a hydrocarbon?
misconceptions.correct: Carbon dioxide and water.
misconceptions.misconception: Complete combustion produces carbon monoxide and water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carbon monoxide is memorable because it is dangerous, so it is recalled ahead of the ordinary product.
misconceptions.correction: Carbon monoxide is a product of incomplete combustion, when oxygen is short. With plenty of oxygen the carbon is fully oxidised to carbon dioxide.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the hydrogen in a burning fuel?
misconceptions.correct: It is oxidised to water.
misconceptions.misconception: The hydrogen is released as hydrogen gas.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The hydrogen has to go somewhere, and coming out unchanged as an element is the simplest fate to imagine.
misconceptions.correction: The hydrogen combines with oxygen and leaves as water. Nothing escapes as hydrogen gas during combustion.

misconceptions.question: What is oxidised when a hydrocarbon burns?
misconceptions.correct: Both the carbon and the hydrogen are oxidised.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the carbon is oxidised; the hydrogen is not involved.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carbon dioxide is the product students name first, so carbon gets the attention and water is treated as a by-product.
misconceptions.correction: Water is an oxide of hydrogen. Both elements in the fuel gain oxygen, and both contribute to the energy released.

misconceptions.question: Does combustion release or absorb energy?
misconceptions.correct: It releases energy.
misconceptions.misconception: Combustion takes in energy, because you have to heat the fuel to start it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ignition genuinely needs energy, and that initial input is mistaken for the overall energy change.
misconceptions.correction: A small input starts the reaction, but combustion releases far more energy than it takes in. That is why fuels are useful.

misconceptions.question: Does a combustion equation need to be balanced?
misconceptions.correct: Yes – every element must have the same number of atoms on each side.
misconceptions.misconception: If the formulae are right the equation is finished; the numbers in front do not matter.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Writing the correct formulae feels like the hard chemistry, so balancing is treated as tidying up.
misconceptions.correction: Atoms are not created or destroyed. CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O has four hydrogens on the left and two on the right, so it is wrong.

misconceptions.question: How do you balance a combustion equation?
misconceptions.correct: Adjust the big numbers until every element matches on both sides.
misconceptions.misconception: Doubling one side of the equation is a way to make it balance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Doubling is the move that fixes odd hydrogen counts in some equations, so it is applied without re-checking the other side.
misconceptions.correction: Any change must be checked against every element on both sides. Doubling the left alone always unbalances what was previously correct.

misconceptions.question: What does cracking do to a hydrocarbon?
misconceptions.correct: It breaks it down into smaller, more useful molecules.
misconceptions.misconception: Cracking joins small molecules together to make bigger ones.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Cracking and polymerisation are both industrial processes involving alkenes, and the direction of change is easily reversed.
misconceptions.correction: Cracking breaks large molecules down. It is polymerisation that joins small alkene molecules into long chains.

misconceptions.question: Is cracking a chemical or a physical change?
misconceptions.correct: Chemical – new, smaller molecules are produced.
misconceptions.misconception: Cracking just separates the molecules that were already there, like distillation does.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Cracking is met immediately after fractional distillation and both are described as ways of processing fractions.
misconceptions.correction: Distillation separates molecules unchanged; cracking breaks covalent bonds and makes molecules that were not present before.

misconceptions.question: Why is cracking carried out?
misconceptions.correct: There is a high demand for fuels with small molecules.
misconceptions.misconception: Demand is highest for the fuels made of large molecules.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Large fractions come out of the column in large quantities, and abundance is confused with demand.
misconceptions.correction: Supply of long-chain fractions exceeds demand, while short-chain fuels such as petrol are in short supply. Cracking converts one into the other.

misconceptions.question: What is the purpose of cracking?
misconceptions.correct: To convert surplus large molecules into smaller, more useful ones.
misconceptions.misconception: Cracking is done to remove sulfur and other impurities from fuels.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Any extra industrial step is assumed to be a purification, because purifying is the reason students most often meet for processing.
misconceptions.correction: Cracking changes the size of the molecules. Removing sulfur is a separate process and is not what cracking is for.

misconceptions.question: What are the two methods of cracking named in the specification?
misconceptions.correct: Catalytic cracking and steam cracking.
misconceptions.misconception: The methods are fractional cracking and electrolytic cracking.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fractional distillation and electrolysis are the process names most recently learned, so they are borrowed to fill the gap.
misconceptions.correction: The specification names catalytic cracking and steam cracking. Neither electrolysis nor distillation is involved.

misconceptions.question: What conditions are used for catalytic cracking?
misconceptions.correct: Hydrocarbon vapour is passed over a hot catalyst.
misconceptions.misconception: Catalytic cracking is carried out cold, because a catalyst removes the need for heat.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Catalysts are taught as a way of speeding up reactions without high temperatures, so heat is assumed to be unnecessary.
misconceptions.correction: A catalyst lowers the energy needed but does not remove it. The hydrocarbon must first be vaporised and the catalyst is hot.

misconceptions.question: What conditions are used for steam cracking?
misconceptions.correct: Vapour is mixed with steam and heated to a very high temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: Steam cracking uses a catalyst and only a mild temperature, because the steam does the work.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Steam is associated with boiling water at 100 °C, which sets an expectation of moderate conditions.
misconceptions.correction: Steam cracking uses no catalyst and a very high temperature – far hotter than boiling water. The steam simply dilutes the hydrocarbon.

misconceptions.question: What types of hydrocarbon does cracking produce?
misconceptions.correct: Alkanes and alkenes.
misconceptions.misconception: Cracking produces only smaller alkanes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The starting material is an alkane, and students expect the products of breaking a molecule up to be the same kind of substance.
misconceptions.correction: There are not enough hydrogen atoms to make every product an alkane, so alkenes are formed as well.

misconceptions.question: What are the products of cracking?
misconceptions.correct: Smaller alkanes and alkenes.
misconceptions.misconception: Cracking produces alcohols, because they are the other organic family.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Alkanes, alkenes and alcohols are three similar-sounding families and the names are interchanged under pressure.
misconceptions.correction: Alcohols contain oxygen. Cracking a hydrocarbon with no oxygen present cannot produce them.

misconceptions.question: How does bromine water distinguish an alkene from an alkane?
misconceptions.correct: Only the alkene reacts with it and decolourises it.
misconceptions.misconception: Both alkanes and alkenes react with bromine water, just at different speeds.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that alkenes are 'more reactive', which suggests a difference of degree rather than a yes/no test.
misconceptions.correction: For this test the alkane gives no reaction and the bromine water stays orange. That is what makes the test useful.

misconceptions.question: What colour change happens when bromine water reacts with an alkene?
misconceptions.correct: Orange to colourless.
misconceptions.misconception: Colourless bromine water turns orange when an alkene is added.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Positive tests are usually remembered as 'a colour appears', so the direction of this change is reversed.
misconceptions.correction: Bromine water starts orange. The alkene reacts with the bromine and removes the colour, so it ends up colourless.

misconceptions.question: What does bromine water look like after reacting with an alkene?
misconceptions.correct: Colourless.
misconceptions.misconception: It turns milky white, or goes cloudy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Limewater going milky is the best-known positive test at GCSE, and its appearance is transferred to this one.
misconceptions.correction: Milky white is the limewater test for carbon dioxide. Bromine water with an alkene simply loses its orange colour.

misconceptions.question: Which hydrocarbons are used to make polymers?
misconceptions.correct: Alkenes.
misconceptions.misconception: Polymers are made from alkanes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Alkanes are the hydrocarbons met most often, so they are offered as the answer to any hydrocarbon question.
misconceptions.correction: Alkanes are saturated and unreactive. It is the more reactive alkenes that join together to form polymers.

misconceptions.question: What are alkenes used for?
misconceptions.correct: To produce polymers and as starting materials for many other chemicals.
misconceptions.misconception: Alkenes are only useful as fuels.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Cracking is introduced as a way of making more fuel, so everything it produces is assumed to be burned.
misconceptions.correction: Cracking does supply fuels, but the alkenes are more valuable as feedstock for polymers and other chemicals.

misconceptions.question: Does cracking increase the amount of crude oil available?
misconceptions.correct: No. It changes the molecules we already have into more useful ones.
misconceptions.misconception: Cracking makes crude oil a renewable resource.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Cracking is described as making more of the fuels we want, which sounds like making more oil.
misconceptions.correction: Cracking cannot create hydrocarbons. It converts a surplus fraction into products in higher demand; crude oil remains finite.

misconceptions.question: Does the petrochemical industry make every industrial chemical?
misconceptions.correct: No. It makes materials from crude oil fractions, such as solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything made by heavy industry – cement, glass, the gases from air – comes from the petrochemical industry.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Chemical industry' is treated as one undivided thing, so the raw material each product actually starts from is never checked.
misconceptions.correction: The petrochemical industry starts from crude oil. Cement and glass start from quarried rock, and nitrogen and oxygen from liquid air.

mcqs.stem: Crude oil is found in rocks. What was crude oil formed from?

options.text: The remains of an ancient biomass consisting mainly of plankton
options.rationale: This is exactly what the specification states: crude oil is the remains of an ancient biomass, mainly plankton, buried in mud.

options.text: The remains of dinosaurs and other large animals buried in mud
options.rationale: 'Fossil fuel' is linked with fossils, and dinosaurs are the fossils students meet first.

options.text: The remains of ancient forests of land plants buried in swamp
options.rationale: This describes how coal formed; one fossil fuel's origin is stretched to cover them all.

options.text: Minerals in the rock that were changed by heat and pressure
options.rationale: Heat and pressure acted on the buried biomass, but crude oil began as living organisms, not minerals.

mcqs.stem: Why is crude oil described as a finite resource?

options.text: New oil is forming at the same rate that we use it
options.rationale: Students hear oil is still forming and assume the supply is being topped up usefully.

options.text: New crude oil forms far more slowly than we use it up
options.rationale: A finite resource is one being consumed much faster than it is replaced, so supplies will run out.

options.text: It is only found in a small number of countries on Earth
options.rationale: 'Finite' is read as limited availability by location rather than limited total quantity.

options.text: It is a mixture, so it cannot be put together again
options.rationale: Being a mixture is why it can be separated; it has nothing to do with why it is finite.

mcqs.stem: What is a hydrocarbon?

options.text: A molecule made of hydrogen, carbon and oxygen atoms
options.rationale: Later organic molecules such as alcohols do contain oxygen, so oxygen feels included.

options.text: Any compound that contains carbon in its molecules
options.rationale: The 'carbon' half of the word is noticed and the 'hydro' half ignored.

options.text: A molecule made of hydrogen and carbon atoms only
options.rationale: The specification defines hydrocarbons as molecules made up of hydrogen and carbon atoms only.

options.text: Any substance that burns to release energy
options.rationale: Hydrogen and ethanol burn well but neither is a hydrocarbon; burning is not the definition.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about crude oil is correct?

options.text: It is one compound with a single fixed formula
options.rationale: One black liquid with one name suggests one substance with one formula.

options.text: It is a compound of carbon and hydrogen only
options.rationale: Knowing it is 'made of carbon and hydrogen' leads students straight to compound.

options.text: It is an element, as it comes from the ground
options.rationale: Being found naturally says nothing about classification; crude oil contains many different molecules.

options.text: It is a mixture of a great many compounds
options.rationale: The specification says crude oil is a mixture of a very large number of compounds, most of them hydrocarbons.

mcqs.stem: What is the general formula for the homologous series of alkanes?

options.text: CₙH₂ₙ — exactly twice as many hydrogens as carbons
options.rationale: CₙH₂ₙ is the tidier pattern and belongs to the alkenes, so the two get swapped.

options.text: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ — twice as many hydrogens as carbons, plus two
options.rationale: This is the general formula given in the specification; methane checks it, since 2 × 1 + 2 = 4.

options.text: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ — twice as many hydrogens as carbon, less two
options.rationale: The '+2' is recalled only as 'a small number', so −2 looks equally reasonable.

options.text: CₙH₂ₙ₊₁ — twice the number of carbons, and one more
options.rationale: CₙH₂ₙ₊₁ is the pattern of an alkyl group, not of a whole alkane molecule.

mcqs.stem: An alkane molecule contains 7 carbon atoms. What is its molecular formula?

options.text: C₇H₉, since 7 + 2 = 9
options.rationale: The 2n is dropped and the +2 is simply added to the number of carbon atoms.

options.text: C₇H₁₅, from CₙH₂ₙ₊₁
options.rationale: The +2 is misremembered as +1, giving the alkyl group pattern instead.

options.text: C₇H₁₆, using CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
options.rationale: With n = 7 the alkane formula gives 2 × 7 + 2 = 16 hydrogen atoms.

options.text: C₇H₁₄, using CₙH₂ₙ
options.rationale: The alkene general formula is used in place of the alkane one.

mcqs.stem: What are the first four members of the alkanes, in order?

options.text: Methane, ethene, propene and butene
options.rationale: The prefixes are shared with the alkenes, so only the -ane ending distinguishes them.

options.text: Methane, ethane, propane, pentane
options.rationale: Pent- sounds like five and is a familiar counting prefix, unlike but-.

options.text: Methane, ethane, butane, octane
options.rationale: The unfamiliar prefix order is guessed at, and butane and octane are the names heard most often.

options.text: Methane, ethane, propane, butane
options.rationale: These are the first four alkanes named by the specification, in order of increasing carbon number.

mcqs.stem: An alkane can be shown as a molecular formula or as a displayed formula. What extra information does the displayed formula give?

options.text: It shows the bonds between the atoms
options.rationale: A displayed formula shows every atom and every covalent bond, which a molecular formula cannot show.

options.text: It shows how many atoms there are of each
options.rationale: Both forms show the same atoms, so the atom count is what stands out.

options.text: It shows the charge on each of the atoms
options.rationale: Charges appear in ionic diagrams, and that habit is carried over to covalent drawings.

options.text: It shows the mass of each atom present
options.rationale: The lines are read as labels for something numerical rather than as bonds.

mcqs.stem: Ethane has the molecular formula C₂H₆. How many covalent bonds are shown in its displayed formula?

options.text: Eight, a C=C bond plus six C–H bonds
options.rationale: Two adjacent carbon atoms suggest a double bond, especially once alkenes have been drawn.

options.text: Six, just the six C–H bonds are drawn
options.rationale: The carbon–carbon bond is overlooked because it joins two atoms of the same element.

options.text: Seven, one C–C bond plus six C–H bonds
options.rationale: The two carbon atoms are joined by one bond, and each carbon holds three hydrogen atoms: 1 + 6 = 7.

options.text: Nine, one bond for each atom shown
options.rationale: Counting atoms is easy and gives a number, so it substitutes for counting bonds.

mcqs.stem: Which of these substances is an alkane?

options.text: C₅H₁₀ — hydrogen atoms = 2 × 5 exactly
options.rationale: The alkene pattern CₙH₂ₙ is accepted as the alkane pattern.

options.text: C₅H₁₂O — it has 12 hydrogen atoms
options.rationale: The hydrogen count matches, so the extra oxygen atom is not treated as disqualifying.

options.text: C₄H₈ — it is also a hydrocarbon
options.rationale: Being a hydrocarbon is confused with being an alkane, and the formula is never tested.

options.text: C₅H₁₂ — hydrogen atoms = 2 × 5 + 2
options.rationale: It fits CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 5, so it is an alkane.

mcqs.stem: Crude oil is separated into fractions by fractional distillation. What is the separation based on?

options.text: Differences in the boiling points of the molecules
options.rationale: Fractional distillation sorts hydrocarbons by the temperature at which their vapour condenses, which depends on boiling point.

options.text: Differences in how fast the molecules react together
options.rationale: Anything happening in a large industrial tower is assumed to be a chemical change.

options.text: Differences in the density of the liquid hydrocarbons
options.rationale: The heaviest fractions are collected lowest, so settling by density looks like enough of an explanation.

options.text: Differences in the colours of the compounds
options.rationale: Colour plays no part; the column separates by temperature, not by appearance.

mcqs.stem: What do the molecules in one fraction of crude oil have in common?

options.text: They are all molecules of exactly the same compound
options.rationale: Fractions have single names like petrol, and named substances usually mean one compound.

options.text: They have a similar number of carbon atoms
options.rationale: The specification defines a fraction as containing molecules with a similar number of carbon atoms.

options.text: They all contain the same number of hydrogen atoms
options.rationale: 'Similar' is upgraded to 'identical', and hydrogen is the larger number in the formula.

options.text: They all have exactly the same boiling point
options.rationale: A fraction boils over a range of temperatures, which is why it is still a mixture.

mcqs.stem: How does fractional distillation separate the hydrocarbons in crude oil?

options.text: The oil is melted, then each fraction freezes out at a different temperature
options.rationale: Melting and freezing are the pair of changes met first, and any temperature separation is mapped onto them.

options.text: The oil is filtered, and the larger molecules are held by a fine mesh
options.rationale: Filtering separates solids from liquids; all the hydrocarbons here are in the same phase.

options.text: The oil is burned, and the gases given off are then collected separately
options.rationale: Burning would destroy the hydrocarbons; a chemical change is assumed to be happening in the column.

options.text: The oil is evaporated, then each fraction condenses at a different temperature
options.rationale: Evaporation followed by condensation at different heights in the column is exactly how the specification requires this to be explained.

mcqs.stem: Why are the fractions containing the largest molecules collected near the bottom of the column?

options.text: They have the highest boiling points, so they condense first
options.rationale: The column is hottest at the bottom, so the fractions with the highest boiling points condense there.

options.text: The bottom of the fractionating column is the coolest part of it
options.rationale: 'Heat rises' is applied to a column that is in fact deliberately cooled towards the top.

options.text: They are the densest, so they sink down to the bottom
options.rationale: The material moving up the column is vapour, not liquid settling out by density.

options.text: They have the lowest boiling points of all fractions
options.rationale: The direction of the boiling point trend is reversed, so the reasoning inverts.

mcqs.stem: What are the fractions from crude oil processed to produce?

options.text: Fuels only, because every fraction is burned as a fuel
options.rationale: Fuels are the use of crude oil students meet at home, so it eclipses the feedstock role.

options.text: Fuels, and feedstock for the petrochemical industry
options.rationale: The specification states that the fractions can be processed to produce fuels and feedstock for the petrochemical industry.

options.text: Fuels only, since feedstock is another word for fuel
options.rationale: The two words sit in the same sentence and both suggest something fed into a process.

options.text: Metals and ceramics used in the building trade
options.rationale: Metals come from ores, not from crude oil fractions.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a fuel produced from crude oil?

options.text: Charcoal, made by heating wood
options.rationale: Charcoal is made from wood, so it is not obtained from crude oil.

options.text: Bioethanol, from fermentation
options.rationale: It is a liquid fuel used in engines, so it is filed alongside petrol without asking where it comes from.

options.text: Kerosene, an aircraft fuel
options.rationale: Kerosene is one of the fuels the specification lists as produced from crude oil.

options.text: Hydrogen, from electrolysis
options.rationale: Hydrogen is a fuel, but it is manufactured rather than separated from crude oil.

mcqs.stem: Which of these are produced by the petrochemical industry?

options.text: Solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents
options.rationale: These are the four examples of useful materials the specification gives for the petrochemical industry.

options.text: Petrol, diesel oil, kerosene and fuel oil
options.rationale: 'Petro-' is read as petrol, so the industry is assumed to be the one that makes it.

options.text: Limestone, cement, sand and glass items
options.rationale: These come from rocks quarried from the ground, not from crude oil.

options.text: Nitrogen, oxygen and argon, taken from air
options.rationale: These are separated from liquid air, a completely different raw material.

mcqs.stem: Why is there such a vast array of natural and synthetic carbon compounds?

options.text: Carbon has far more isotopes than any other element does
options.rationale: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are well known, so isotopes come to mind first.

options.text: Carbon atoms can form families of similar compounds
options.rationale: The specification attributes the huge number of carbon compounds to carbon's ability to form families of similar compounds.

options.text: Carbon atoms bond ionically to form long chains
options.rationale: Ionic bonding is the strong bonding met first, so it is offered whenever strong bonds are needed.

options.text: Carbon is the most abundant element in the Earth
options.rationale: Carbon is not especially abundant; it is its bonding, not its quantity, that matters.

mcqs.stem: Some properties of hydrocarbons depend on the size of their molecules. Which set of properties is this?

options.text: Boiling point, solubility and conductivity
options.rationale: Any plausible list of properties is accepted when the specific three are not memorised.

options.text: Colour, density and electrical conductivity
options.rationale: Hydrocarbons do not conduct at all, so conductivity cannot show a trend.

options.text: Boiling point, viscosity and flammability
options.rationale: These are the three properties the specification names as depending on molecular size.

options.text: Density, hardness and melting point
options.rationale: Hardness is not a property of a liquid fuel and is outside the trends required.

mcqs.stem: How do the properties of hydrocarbons change as the molecules get larger?

options.text: Boiling point down, viscosity up, flammability down
options.rationale: The boiling point trend alone is reversed, which is the single most common slip.

options.text: Boiling point rises, viscosity down, flammability up
options.rationale: Viscosity is guessed at from pouring heavy things, and more carbon is assumed to burn better.

options.text: Boiling point falls, viscosity falls, flammability up
options.rationale: All three trends are inverted, treating small molecules as the 'heavy duty' ones.

options.text: Boiling point up, viscosity up, flammability down
options.rationale: Larger molecules attract each other more strongly, so they boil higher and flow less easily, and they are harder to ignite.

mcqs.stem: How does the boiling point of a hydrocarbon change as its molecules get larger?

options.text: It decreases, as larger molecules are heavier and move slower
options.rationale: Heaviness is used to argue for easier escape, reversing the real trend.

options.text: It increases, as larger molecules attract each other more strongly
options.rationale: More energy is needed to separate larger molecules, so the boiling point rises with molecular size.

options.text: It stays the same, as they are all hydrocarbon molecules
options.rationale: Belonging to one family is taken to mean identical physical properties.

options.text: It rises at first and then falls again for long chains
options.rationale: There is no turning point in this trend; boiling point rises throughout.

mcqs.stem: How does the viscosity of a hydrocarbon change as its molecules get larger?

options.text: It increases, so the liquid catches fire faster
options.rationale: Viscosity, volatility and flammability blur into one vague idea about fuel behaviour.

options.text: It decreases, so the liquid flows freely
options.rationale: Viscosity is guessed at from everyday experience of pouring heavy things.

options.text: It increases, so the liquid flows less easily
options.rationale: Longer molecules attract and tangle with each other more, so thick fractions pour very slowly.

options.text: It is the same for all liquid hydrocarbons
options.rationale: Petrol and heavy fuel oil pour very differently, so viscosity clearly varies.

mcqs.stem: How does the flammability of a hydrocarbon change as its molecules get larger?

options.text: It increases, as there is more carbon to burn
options.rationale: More fuel per molecule sounds like more burning, confusing energy released with ease of ignition.

options.text: It increases, so it is easier to set alight
options.rationale: The trend is simply inverted, with size read as 'more powerful fuel'.

options.text: It does not change for any hydrocarbon
options.rationale: Petrol lights instantly while heavy fuel oil needs preheating, so flammability clearly varies.

options.text: It decreases, so it is harder to ignite
options.rationale: Large molecules are hard to vaporise, and a fuel must vaporise before it will burn.

mcqs.stem: Liquefied petroleum gases are used in portable camping stoves. Which property makes them suitable?

options.text: They are highly flammable and ignite very easily
options.rationale: Small hydrocarbon molecules vaporise readily and are highly flammable, which is exactly what a small stove needs.

options.text: They have high boiling points and do not evaporate
options.rationale: Not evaporating sounds safe, so a high boiling point is assumed to be desirable.

options.text: They are very viscous and pour out slowly and safely
options.rationale: Viscosity is treated as a safety feature rather than as a property of large molecules.

options.text: They contain the largest hydrocarbon molecules of all
options.rationale: Large molecules are assumed to be the most powerful fuels, so they are chosen for a stove.

mcqs.stem: What happens when a hydrocarbon undergoes complete combustion?

options.text: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen form, and energy is taken in
options.rationale: The hydrogen is imagined leaving unchanged, and ignition energy is mistaken for the overall change.

options.text: Carbon monoxide and water form, and energy is released
options.rationale: Carbon monoxide is memorable because it is dangerous, so it is recalled ahead of carbon dioxide.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water form, and heat energy is released
options.rationale: The specification states that complete combustion produces carbon dioxide and water, and that combustion releases energy.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water form, and energy is taken in
options.rationale: A small energy input is needed to start the reaction, and that is mistaken for the overall change.

mcqs.stem: During the combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel, what happens to the carbon and the hydrogen?

options.text: Only the carbon is oxidised, not the hydrogen
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide is named first, so water is treated as a mere by-product.

options.text: Both are reduced, because both lose oxygen
options.rationale: Oxygen is gained here, not lost, so this is oxidation and not reduction.

options.text: Only the hydrogen is oxidised, to water
options.rationale: Water is the obvious oxide, so the carbon is assumed to be left over.

options.text: Both are oxidised, because both gain oxygen
options.rationale: The carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide and the hydrogen is oxidised to water, so both gain oxygen.

mcqs.stem: Which equation shows the complete combustion of methane, CH₄?

options.text: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
options.rationale: Carbon: 1 and 1. Hydrogen: 4 and 4. Oxygen: 4 and 4. The equation is balanced.

options.text: 2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 4H₂O
options.rationale: The left side has been doubled without re-checking oxygen: 6 atoms on the left against 8 on the right.

options.text: 2CH₄ + 4O₂ → CO₂ + 4H₂O
options.rationale: The methane has been doubled but the carbon dioxide has not, so carbon no longer balances.

options.text: CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
options.rationale: The formulae are correct but nothing has been balanced: 4 hydrogen atoms on the left, 2 on the right.

mcqs.stem: Which equation shows the complete combustion of propane, C₃H₈?

options.text: 2C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 6CO₂ + 8H₂O
options.rationale: The propane has been doubled but the oxygen has not: 10 oxygen atoms on the left against 20 on the right.

options.text: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O
options.rationale: Carbon: 3 and 3. Hydrogen: 8 and 8. Oxygen: 10 and 10. The equation is balanced.

options.text: 2C₃H₈ + 10O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O
options.rationale: The left side has been doubled and the right side left alone, so carbon and hydrogen both fail.

options.text: 2C₃H₈ + 10O₂ → 6CO₂ + 10H₂O
options.rationale: Carbon balances but hydrogen does not: 16 atoms on the left against 20 on the right.

mcqs.stem: Ethane has the formula C₂H₆. Which equation shows its complete combustion?

options.text: C₂H₆ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O
options.rationale: Carbon and hydrogen balance, but oxygen does not: 6 atoms on the left against 7 on the right.

options.text: C₂H₆ + O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O
options.rationale: Only the products have been balanced; the oxygen on the left was never adjusted.

options.text: C₂H₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
options.rationale: The formulae are right but no balancing has been attempted at all.

options.text: 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O
options.rationale: Carbon: 4 and 4. Hydrogen: 12 and 12. Oxygen: 14 and 14. Doubling the ethane avoids a half-molecule of oxygen.

mcqs.stem: What happens to hydrocarbon molecules during cracking?

options.text: They are broken down into smaller, more useful molecules
options.rationale: The specification defines cracking as breaking hydrocarbons down to produce smaller, more useful molecules.

options.text: They are separated from one another without being changed
options.rationale: Cracking follows fractional distillation, so it is assumed to be another separation.

options.text: They are joined together to make much larger molecules
options.rationale: Cracking and polymerisation both involve alkenes, so the direction of change is reversed.

options.text: They are burned to release energy and carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Burning destroys the hydrocarbons; cracking converts them into other hydrocarbons.

mcqs.stem: Why are the fractions with the largest molecules cracked?

options.text: Fuels made of large molecules are in much higher demand
options.rationale: Long-chain fractions come out of the column in large quantities, and abundance is confused with demand.

options.text: There is a high demand for fuels with small molecules
options.rationale: Cracking converts a surplus of long-chain molecules into short-chain fuels that are in high demand.

options.text: It is the only way to remove the sulfur from these fuels
options.rationale: Any extra industrial step is assumed to be a purification.

options.text: It turns each fraction into one pure single compound
options.rationale: Fractions are wrongly imagined as needing to be purified into single compounds.

mcqs.stem: Which two methods of cracking does the specification name?

options.text: Catalytic cracking and fractional cracking
options.rationale: Fractional distillation is the process most recently learned, so its name is borrowed.

options.text: Steam cracking and electrolytic cracking
options.rationale: Electrolysis is another named industrial process and is offered to fill the gap.

options.text: Catalytic cracking and steam cracking
options.rationale: These are the two methods the specification names.

options.text: Thermal cracking and pressure cracking
options.rationale: These sound like plausible industrial names but are not the two the specification gives.

mcqs.stem: What conditions are used for catalytic cracking?

options.text: Hydrocarbons are vaporised and passed over a hot catalyst
options.rationale: In catalytic cracking the hydrocarbon is turned into a vapour and passed over a hot catalyst.

options.text: Hydrocarbons are vaporised and mixed with steam only
options.rationale: The conditions for the two methods of cracking are swapped over.

options.text: Hydrocarbons are cooled and poured over a cold catalyst
options.rationale: Catalysts are taught as removing the need for high temperatures, so heat seems unnecessary.

options.text: Hydrocarbons are dissolved in water with a catalyst
options.rationale: Hydrocarbons are insoluble in water, so this could not be done.

mcqs.stem: What conditions are used for steam cracking?

options.text: The vapour is mixed with steam and then passed over a hot catalyst bed
options.rationale: A catalyst is added to a method that does not use one, blending the two techniques.

options.text: The vapour is mixed with steam and heated to a very high temperature
options.rationale: Steam cracking mixes hydrocarbon vapour with steam and heats it to a very high temperature, with no catalyst.

options.text: The vapour is mixed with steam and kept at a mild temperature
options.rationale: Steam is associated with boiling water at 100 °C, suggesting moderate conditions.

options.text: The liquid is mixed with water and warmed gently in a flask
options.rationale: The process is imagined at laboratory scale rather than as a high temperature industrial one.

mcqs.stem: The products of cracking include alkanes. What is the other type of hydrocarbon produced?

options.text: Only more alkanes, but smaller in size
options.rationale: The starting material is an alkane, so the products are expected to be the same kind of substance.

options.text: Alcohols, that contain oxygen as well
options.rationale: Alkanes, alkenes and alcohols sound alike and the names are interchanged.

options.text: Alkenes, a more reactive hydrocarbon
options.rationale: The specification states that the products of cracking include alkanes and another type of hydrocarbon called alkenes.

options.text: Polymers, made of very long chains
options.rationale: Polymers are associated with cracking because alkenes link the two ideas.

mcqs.stem: How can you show that a hydrocarbon is an alkene and not an alkane?

options.text: Add bromine water; both will react
options.rationale: 'More reactive' is read as a difference of speed rather than a yes-or-no result.

options.text: Add universal indicator and then wait
options.rationale: Indicators are the familiar way of identifying a substance, so they are offered here.

options.text: Add a lit splint and listen for the pop
options.rationale: The squeaky pop test detects hydrogen gas, not a double bond.

options.text: Add bromine water and shake well
options.rationale: Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes and react with bromine water, which is why it is used as the test.

mcqs.stem: What colour change is seen when bromine water reacts with an alkene?

options.text: Colourless bromine water turns orange in colour
options.rationale: Positive tests are usually remembered as a colour appearing, so the direction is reversed.

options.text: Orange bromine water is decolourised to colourless
options.rationale: Bromine water starts orange, and the alkene reacts with the bromine so the colour disappears.

options.text: Orange bromine water turns a cloudy white colour
options.rationale: Limewater going milky is the best known positive test and its appearance is transferred.

options.text: Orange bromine water turns a blue-black colour
options.rationale: Blue-black is the starch test for iodine, a different test entirely.

mcqs.stem: What are alkenes used for?

options.text: Only as fuels for cars, lorries and aeroplanes
options.rationale: Cracking is introduced as a way of making more fuel, so everything it produces is assumed to be burned.

options.text: Nothing much, as polymers come from alkanes
options.rationale: Alkanes are the hydrocarbons met most often, so they are offered as the answer.

options.text: To produce polymers and many other chemicals
options.rationale: The specification states that alkenes are used to produce polymers and as starting materials for many other chemicals.

options.text: To make metals and ceramic building parts
options.rationale: Metals come from ores and ceramics from clay; neither involves alkenes.

mcqs.stem: Cracking one molecule of C₁₀H₂₂ produces one molecule of C₂H₄. What is the other product?

options.text: C₈H₁₆, because an alkene is the product
options.rationale: The product is assumed to match the alkene, so two hydrogen atoms go missing.

options.text: C₁₀H₁₈, since only hydrogen is removed
options.rationale: Only the hydrogen count is adjusted, leaving 12 carbon atoms on the product side.

options.text: C₁₂H₂₆, adding the two formulae up
options.rationale: Cracking is treated as joining molecules, so the formulae are added instead of subtracted.

options.text: C₈H₁₈, so that all the atoms balance
options.rationale: Carbon: 10 = 8 + 2. Hydrogen: 22 = 18 + 4. The equation balances.

mcqs.stem: Give one reason why cracking is useful.

options.text: It turns surplus large molecules into fuels
options.rationale: Cracking converts long-chain fractions that are in low demand into short-chain fuels that are in high demand.

options.text: It makes crude oil into a renewable resource
options.rationale: Making more of the fuels we want sounds like making more oil.

options.text: It removes all of the carbon dioxide from fuel
options.rationale: Any extra industrial step is assumed to clean the fuel up.

options.text: It joins up small molecules to make long chains
options.rationale: The direction of the change is reversed, confusing cracking with polymerisation.
